data.raw_text:
U.S. Army Sergeant John Randolph McKinney of Woodcliff, Georgia, was awarded  the Medal of Honor for his extraordinary actions on May 11, 1945, in Luzon, the Philippines.

McKinney enlisted in the Army in November 1942 from Screven County, Georgia. By May 11th, 1945, he was serving as a private in Company A, 123rd Infantry, 33rd Infantry Division. US Army Pvt. John McKinney had stood guard duty and had just gone to his tent in the early hours of May 11, 1945, on the island of Luzon, Philippines. The vanguard of a Japanese force slipped past the guard post. Sgt. Fukutaro Morii threw McKinney's tent flap open and slashed down with his sword to minimize the sound of the undetected attack. He severed part of McKinney's ear. McKinney, a skilled hunter from Georgia, grabbed the rifle he slept with, bashed Morii in the chin and finished him off with another blow to the head.

Over the next 36 minutes, McKinney protected the flank of his company and his sleeping comrades by killing 38 of the enemy. McKinney did so through point-blank, kill-or-be-killed encounters and rapid-fire, accurate shots with various M1 rifles he picked up and fired at charging enemies. Early in the engagement, he returned to his foxhole, where he eliminated first one wave and then part of the second wave of the main attack force. Several in the second wave made it to the foxhole, where McKinney first shot and then clubbed his assailants in hand-to-hand combat.

He was awarded the Medal of Honor for his actions on this day. McKinney died in April 1997 and is buried at Double Heads Baptist Church in Sylvania, Georgia.

#WeRememberThem

data.raw_text:
DEATH IS NOT FACED THE SAME WAY EVERYWHERE:

1. Mexico: Día de los Muertos is not mourning. It is a reunion. Families build altars and talk to those who left. Death here is an annual visit.

2. Japan: Family washes the body. Mourners pass bones with chopsticks during cremation. The dead receive a new name to enter the next world renewed.

3. Indonesia — Toraja: Bodies kept at home for months or years. Spoken to daily. Considered sick rather than gone. Death waits for the living to be ready.

4. Ghana: Fantasy coffins. A fisherman buried in a wooden fish. A farmer in a cocoa pod. The coffin is a final statement. Funerals last for days.

5. Tibet: Sky burials. Body offered to vultures on a mountaintop. Once the soul departs the body is empty. Nature receives it completely.

6. South Korea: Ashes compressed into decorative beads. Blue. Green. Pink. Displayed at home. The dead become something beautiful the living see every day.

7. New Orleans: Jazz funerals. Procession to the cemetery is mournful. Procession away is loud and dancing. Grief honored then transformed into joy the same afternoon.

8. Madagascar — Famadihana: Families dig up ancestral bones, wrap them in fresh silk and dance with them. The dead are still family. Just in a different form.

9. Ireland: The wake. Body lies at home while family eat, drink and laugh loudly in the same room. The deceased is discussed as though still listening.

10. India — Hindu tradition: Eldest son lights the pyre. Body returns to fire within 24 hours. Thirteen days of mourning follow. Grief has a structure. Structure gives grief somewhere to go.

11. Ancient Egypt: Death was the most important journey of a person's life. Tombs filled with everything the soul might need. Life was rehearsal. Death was the main event.

12. Philippines: Funerals last nine nights. Card games through the night. The community stays until nobody sits with sorrow alone.

13. Zoroastrian tradition: Body placed in a Tower of Silence open to the sky. Fire, earth and water too sacred for death to touch. Nature receives what remains.

14. Vikings: Warriors burned on longships at sea. Buried with everything they owned. Death was continuation into another existence that deserved equal preparation.

15. Aboriginal Australia: The deceased's name not spoken for months or years. Grief has protocols sixty thousand years old. Healing has its own timeline.

16. Thailand — Buddhist tradition: Monks chant for days. Merit made through generosity. Death is not tragedy. It is transition. What truly mattered was never lost.

17. China: White is mourning. Paper replicas of homes and money burned for the afterlife. The dead remain part of family decisions for generations.

18. Jewish tradition: Burial within 24 hours. Then shiva. Seven days where the bereaved do nothing. The community comes to them. Grief is given a room and a witness.

19. Ancient Greece: Coins placed on the eyes to pay the ferryman. Without payment the soul wandered a hundred years. Even death had its economy.

20. Brazil: Funerals move fast. Mourning runs long and loud. Death removes presence. It never removes influence.

21. Korea — Confucian tradition: Ancestral rites on death anniversaries. Tables set with the deceased's favorite food. The bond between living and dead never ends at burial.

22. Ancient Rome: Actors wore ancestor masks in funeral processions. How you were buried announced who you had been.

23. West Africa: Death anniversaries are bigger than the original funeral. Grief transforms into celebration of what was given rather than mourning of what was taken.

24. New Guinea — Dani people: Women historically cut off finger joints at loss of a family member. Grief made permanently visible. The community carried it together.

25. Sudan — Nuer people: An elder's death received with stillness. Considered completion not tragedy. The response calibrated entirely to the life that came before.
